taxonomy_note: Sugra editorial taxonomy for navigating the collected catalog. It is not an international standard and not a claim that the whole industry has exactly 20 directions. One primary direction per family; overlaps are expressed by tags. A family is not a unit for comparing results: compare a specific test version and a compatible protocol.

comparison_policy.default_view: one official publication at a time
comparison_policy.score_selection: preserve every reported observation; never choose max automatically
comparison_policy.cross_source_view: show all observations with publication and settings, no implied same-protocol ranking
comparison_policy.percent: only unit percent gets a % sign; fraction conversion must be explicit
comparison_policy.categories: Sugra editorial taxonomy; not an industry standard

categories.description_en: Tasks a professional is paid for: legal analysis, finance and tax questions, office documents, spreadsheets, research memos and other desk work. The tests here hand the model a realistic brief and judge the finished product, often with a human expert or an expert-written rubric.

Changing and repairing real programs. The model works inside a repository or a terminal over many steps, reads the code, runs commands, and is scored on whether the resulting change passes hidden tests or a reviewer. This is the busiest category on every launch page.

Training and improving models rather than ordinary software: reproducing a research paper, running an experiment, tuning a training recipe, writing a compute kernel. The score is usually whether the resulting artifact works or reaches a target.

Mathematics from contest problems to research-level questions, plus scientific reasoning and laboratory knowledge in chemistry, physics and biology. Dangerous biological capabilities are kept out of this category and sit under Biosecurity.

Finding, matching and using information spread across very long inputs: hundreds of thousands or a million tokens of documents, transcripts or structured data. The tests plant facts or relationships deep in the input and check whether the model can still use them.

Operating a computer the way a person does: a desktop, a browser, a mobile device, through screenshots and clicks rather than an API. Tasks are everyday chores in real applications, scored on whether the end state is correct. Open-ended web research has its own category.
Images, charts, video, audio, scanned documents and sheet music, and reasoning that connects them with text. The model has to read what it sees or hears and answer about it.

Finding and fixing vulnerabilities, reproducing known flaws in controlled test environments, analysing binaries and operating production systems under failure. These tests measure capability in a sandbox; the safety category measures whether the model refuses to misuse it.

Broad knowledge, logic and abstract problem solving, factual accuracy and the mixed question sets that try to cover everything at once. The benchmarks here are the ones most often quoted as a single headline number.
Writing code from a specification without a long agentic process: a function, a component, a drawing, an algorithm. Scored by tests, by rendering the output, or by a judge comparing candidates.

Calling functions and APIs, chaining tools, planning multi-step work and carrying a long task to the end. The environments range from office automation to games, and the score is whether the whole workflow completed.
Finding hard-to-locate facts on the open web and synthesising an answer from many pages. The questions are built so that no single page answers them.
Obeying constraints: output formats, length limits, data schemas, forbidden words and multi-step user requirements. The score is how many constraints the answer honoured.
Knowledge and task performance across natural languages other than English. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
Creative and editorial writing, style, role play, and the emotional and social quality of a conversation. No publication in the catalog has printed a result here yet.
Clinical and medical knowledge, medical documents, and the quality and safety of help given in a medical conversation, usually graded against rubrics written by physicians.

Tests of dangerous biological capability and of dual-use risk: virology know-how, wet-lab troubleshooting, and whether the model refuses requests that could help build a weapon. Some sets also cover chemical and cyber risk. Here a high capability score is not good news, and the refusal scores are the ones to read.

Refusals of harmful requests, resistance to jailbreaks, honesty under pressure, sycophancy, and whether an agent discloses its own failures or takes forbidden shortcuts. Most of these are rates where lower is better; the table says so on each row.
CAD modelling, electrical engineering, spatial design and the production of engineering artifacts from a specification, scored on whether the artifact meets the spec.

Head-to-head preference rankings by people or judge models, and composite indexes that average many unrelated tests into one number. A specialised index stays in its own category; only the catch-all ones live here.

about.what_it_tests: Terminal-Bench tests whether an AI agent can finish real jobs by typing commands into a Linux terminal, such as building software, configuring a system or processing files. Each task runs in its own sandboxed container, and the agent succeeds only if the final state of that container passes the task's automatic checks. Version 2.0 (November 2025) has 89 hand-checked tasks, and the companion Harbor framework runs the agents.
about.notes: Maintainer detail: run through the Harbor framework. Project leads named in the repository README: Ryan Marten, Alex Shaw, Andy Konwinski, Ludwig Schmidt. Maintainers and sandboxed-container design come from the GitHub README. The May 19, 2025 launch date comes from a tbench.ai page seen only in search snippets. The Version 2.0 facts (89 tasks, November 7, 2025) come from secondary coverage. The README does not describe scoring; the leaderboard is on Harbor Hub.

about.what_it_tests: GPQA is a set of 448 multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by experts with or working toward PhDs in those fields. Domain experts reached about 65% accuracy, while skilled non-experts with web access reached about 34%, which is why the questions are described as hard to answer by search alone. The Diamond subset is a smaller, harder selection of these questions.

about.what_it_tests: Humanity's Last Exam is a test of about 2,500 expert-level questions across dozens of subjects, including mathematics, the humanities and the natural sciences. It was built because leading models had passed more than 90 percent of older tests, and at launch the most capable models scored below 10 percent.

Question counts differ by source (2,500 in the paper; about 3,000 in press coverage), so the paper's figure is used. The family label 'HLE with tools' is a configuration of the same benchmark and is not described separately.

about.what_it_tests: The AIME (American Invitational Mathematics Examination) is the second round of the MAA competition series for high-school students in the United States: 15 problems in three hours, each with an integer answer from 0 to 999. As a benchmark, a given year's two exams (30 problems) are posed to a model, and the score is the share answered correctly; publishers state whether tools such as a Python interpreter were allowed.
about.notes: The exam has run since 1983; the benchmark use is a publisher convention and the introduced year is left empty. The year in a label (AIME 2024, AIME 2025) matters: newer exams are less likely to appear in training data. Attempt counts differ between publishers.

about.what_it_tests: AutomationBench tests whether AI agents can carry out business workflows that span several software applications, such as a CRM, an inbox, a calendar and a messaging tool, through their REST APIs. The agent has to find the right endpoints on its own, follow layered business rules, and ignore misleading records along the way. Grading is programmatic: the final state of the simulated systems is checked against success criteria, so a run is judged on the end result.
about.notes: Maintainer detail: (paper authors Daniel Shepard and Robin Salimans); Artificial Analysis runs the AutomationBench-AA leaderboard in partnership with Zapier. The benchmark has several versions and scores differ by version and source: the Zapier public leaderboard, the Artificial Analysis guardrail-based AutomationBench-AA (657 private tasks, announced July 6, 2026), and BenchLM private-set figures are not comparable. The arXiv abstract says even the best frontier models scored below 10 percent at release. The printed-by labels (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba) were not checked against model cards.

about.what_it_tests: LiveCodeBench tests whether a code model can solve competitive programming problems it could not have seen in training. It collects new problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder and Codeforces contests, and each problem carries a release date, so models can be tested on problems released after their training cutoff. Beyond code generation, the benchmark covers self-repair, test output prediction and code execution. The release_v6 set holds 1,055 problems published between May 2023 and April 2025, and publishers print pass@1, scored by running generated code against test cases with a modified version of the APPS checker.
about.notes: The GitHub README (fetched, undated) lists release_v1 through release_v6, with release_v6 at 1,055 problems and an end date of April 2025, and describes pass@1 and pass@5. The arXiv abstract (submitted 12 March 2024, lead author Naman Jain) gives the 400-problem first release and the four scenarios, but it does not describe v6. The README names release_v6 rather than the label v6 printed on model cards, and no fetched page confirms that mapping, so cite the release by its date range and count.

about.what_it_tests: CWE-Bench evaluates coding agents on defensive security work. Each task gives the agent a checkout of a real open-source repository, sometimes with disclosed CVEs reproduced in it, and asks it to audit the code and fix what it finds without being told how many vulnerabilities there are. A fix counts only if the exploit is blocked and the existing tests still pass, with no partial credit, and agents are not asked to write exploits. The page reports 100 held-out tasks in v0 and 120 in v1.
about.notes: Maintainer and method are from the cwe-bench.com page, which cites Collinear AI as author and names Artificial Analysis as the independent evaluator that ran the published results. The page lists v0 on Sept 1 and v1 on Sept 25, and its citations give 2026, which is where the year comes from. The printed label says Google, and no Google source was found, so that attribution is unconfirmed; an aggregator naming a Google model as top scorer is a leaderboard fact, not a maintainer fact. The page has no separate paper. The v1 three-judge panel is reported beside the deterministic score, not in place of it. No scores are given.

about.what_it_tests: ExploitBench measures how far an AI agent gets along a ladder of 16 checkable capability steps when it works on known, already-patched bugs in the V8 JavaScript engine used by Chromium. about.what_it_tests: Legal Research Bench tests whether an AI agent can answer realistic US legal research questions, using tools such as case-law search, web search and document retrieval to produce a supported answer. about.what_it_tests: Code Arena, earlier called WebDev Arena, is a live human-preference leaderboard for building web applications. about.what_it_tests: BioMysteryBench tests whether a model can do real bioinformatics research work on messy real-world data. about.notes: The arXiv paper (25 May 2022, Alexis Conneau and co-authors) describes the corpus; its abstract does not name the metrics. A model card that prints a small decimal with "lower is better" and no metric name is stored as a fraction with that note.

families.name: FRAMES
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: FRAMES (Fact, Fetch, and Reason) tests whether a model can answer multi-hop questions that need facts from several web sources combined by reasoning. It is used to evaluate retrieval-augmented and search-agent setups. The score is the share of questions answered correctly.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (19 September 2024) describes the questions and the accuracy score. Publishers print the accuracy either as a fraction or as a percentage.

families.name: DSBench (DeepSeek internal)
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: DSBench is a pair of internal DeepSeek test sets: DSBench-FullStack holds full-stack development tasks and DSBench-Hard holds difficult coding-agent problems. The tasks and the scoring are not published.
about.notes: The only description is the footnote on the DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 and V4-Flash-0731 model cards.

families.name: AGIEval
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: AGIEval tests general ability with questions taken from standardized human exams: college entrance tests, law school admission tests, math competitions and lawyer qualification exams, in English and Chinese. The score is the share of questions answered correctly.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (13 April 2023) describes the exam sources. Model cards usually print it as exact-match accuracy with a stated number of shots.

families.name: C-Eval
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Tsinghua University (Yuzhen Huang and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: C-Eval tests knowledge and reasoning in Chinese with multiple-choice questions from 52 disciplines at four levels: middle school, high school, college and professional. The score is accuracy over the question set.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (15 May 2023) describes the levels and disciplines.

families.name: CMMLU
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: MBZUAI and partners (Haonan Li and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: CMMLU tests knowledge and reasoning in Chinese across natural sciences, social sciences, engineering and the humanities, in the multiple-choice format of MMLU. The score is accuracy; random guessing scores 25 percent.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (15 June 2023) describes the subjects and the few-shot and chain-of-thought settings.

families.name: MultiLoKo
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: MultiLoKo tests multilingual knowledge with 500 locally relevant questions in each of 31 languages, plus translated versions that show how much an answer depends on the language of the question. Publishers print the average score across languages.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (14 April 2025) describes the languages and the parity measures; the abstract does not fix one scoring metric, so a printed value is stored with the metric label the publisher used.

families.name: FACTS Parametric
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: FACTS Parametric is the closed-book part of the FACTS Benchmark Suite: trivia-style factual questions that a model must answer from its own knowledge, without search or other tools. It has public and private question sets of 1,052 items each, and the score is accuracy.
about.notes: The Google DeepMind announcement (9 December 2025) describes the four parts of the suite; Kaggle holds the private sets and the leaderboard. A model card that prints "FACTS Parametric" with a shot count ran the public set itself.

families.name: TriviaQA
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: University of Washington (Mandar Joshi and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: TriviaQA tests reading comprehension and recall with about 95,000 trivia questions written by enthusiasts, each paired with evidence documents. Model cards usually print exact-match accuracy on the answers, often without the evidence documents, which turns it into a knowledge test.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (9 May 2017) describes the question collection. The setting a card used (with or without evidence documents) is stored with the observation when stated.

families.name: DROP
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI and UC Irvine (Dheeru Dua and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: DROP tests reading comprehension that needs discrete reasoning over a paragraph: resolving references, then adding, counting, comparing or sorting what the paragraph says. The score is a token-level F1 between the answer and the reference, printed as a percentage.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (1 March 2019) describes the operations and the F1 score.

families.name: HellaSwag
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI (Rowan Zellers and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: HellaSwag tests commonsense inference: the model reads the start of an everyday situation and picks the most plausible continuation from several candidates, where the wrong ones were machine-written to fool models. The score is accuracy.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (19 May 2019) describes the adversarial construction.

families.name: WinoGrande
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: Allen Institute for AI (Keisuke Sakaguchi and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: WinoGrande tests commonsense reasoning with 44,000 pronoun-resolution problems in the style of the Winograd Schema Challenge, built at scale and filtered to remove shortcuts. The score is the share of problems answered correctly.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (24 July 2019) describes the construction and the bias reduction.

families.name: CLUEWSC
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: CLUE benchmark team (Liang Xu and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: CLUEWSC is the Winograd Schema task of the CLUE Chinese language understanding benchmark: the model decides which noun a pronoun in a Chinese sentence refers to. The score is accuracy.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (13 April 2020) describes the nine CLUE tasks; the Winograd task is one of them. Model cards print it on its own as CLUEWSC.

families.name: BigCodeBench
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.

about.maintainer: BigCode project (Terry Yue Zhuo and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: BigCodeBench tests code generation with 1,140 Python tasks that need calls into 139 libraries across seven domains, each checked by several unit tests. The score is the share of tasks whose generated code passes all tests.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (22 June 2024) describes the tasks and the test coverage.

families.name: CMATH

families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: CMATH tests elementary-school math in Chinese with about 1,700 word problems from workbooks and exams across six grades. The score is accuracy, which the paper also reports per grade.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (29 June 2023) describes the grades and the distractor test.

families.name: Chinese SimpleQA
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: Taobao and Tmall Group (Yancheng He and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: Chinese SimpleQA tests factual recall in Chinese with short questions across six topics and 99 subtopics. An LLM grader marks each answer correct or not, and the score is the share answered correctly.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (11 November 2024) describes the topics and the grading. Cards print it as Chinese-SimpleQA or C-SimpleQA.

families.name: IMO-AnswerBench
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.what_it_tests: IMO-AnswerBench is the short-answer part of IMO-Bench: 400 Olympiad-level problems whose answers can be checked automatically. The score is the share of problems answered correctly.
about.notes: The arXiv paper "Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning" (3 November 2025) describes the three IMO-Bench parts; the proof and grading parts are separate benchmarks.

families.name: CorpusQA
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.
families.vendor_flags_scope: 15 inspected official publications; blank does not mean never used

about.maintainer: Alibaba Tongyi Lab (Zhiyuan Lu and co-authors)
about.what_it_tests: CorpusQA tests reasoning over whole document collections: the evidence for a question is spread over hundreds of files, and the answer needs comparison or aggregation rather than lookup. Inputs scale up to about 10 million tokens; publishers usually print the 1 million token setting as accuracy.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (21 January 2026) describes the synthetic queries and programmatic answers; its abstract does not fix one metric, so a printed value keeps the metric label the publisher used.

families.name: BrowseComp-ZH
families.classification_note: Editorial assignment by test subject and source catalog; version, protocol and result metric remain separate fields.

about.what_it_tests: BrowseComp-ZH tests web browsing on the Chinese internet with 289 multi-hop questions across 11 domains, each built backwards from a short objective answer. The score is accuracy.
about.notes: The arXiv paper (27 April 2025) describes the question construction.

publications.coverage: The eleven eval tables at the end of the page (Professional, Coding, Science and health, Computer use, Cybersecurity, Self-improvement, Multimodal, Academic, Tool use, Long context, Abstract reasoning) and the footnotes they cite. Left out: the interactive cost, latency and multi-agent charts, the prose claims, pricing and availability.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.5
publications.coverage: The eight tables of the Evaluations section (Coding, Professional, Computer use and vision, Tool use, Academic, Cybersecurity, Long context, Abstract reasoning) with their row notes and the closing note on reasoning effort. Left out: the prose claims, the charts in the body and pricing.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.4
publications.coverage: The eight tables of the Evaluations section (Professional, Coding, Computer use and vision, Tool use, Academic, Long context, Abstract reasoning, Evals without reasoning) and the closing note on reasoning effort. The five-row summary table at the top repeats values from these tables and its OSWorld note is kept on that observation. Left out: the GDPval wins-and-ties chart, the prose claims, the charts in the body and pricing.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.4 mini and nano
publications.coverage: The five tables at the end of the page (Coding, Tool-calling, Intelligence, MM / Vision / CUA, Long context) with their two footnotes. The five-row table at the top repeats values from them. Left out: the accuracy-versus-latency and accuracy-versus-cost charts, the prose claims and pricing.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.3-Codex
publications.coverage: The six-row Appendix table and its footnote. The bar charts in the body (SWE-Bench Pro accuracy versus output tokens, Terminal-Bench 2.0) repeat Appendix values and are not transcribed separately. Left out: the prose claims and the OSWorld and GDPval charts without printed values.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.2
publications.coverage: The Appendix "Detailed benchmarks" (Professional, Coding, Factuality, Long context, Vision, Tool usage, Academic, Abstract reasoning) with its two notes, and the Mental health evaluations table in the Safety section. The ten-row table at the top of the page and the GDPval chart repeat Appendix values. Left out: the relative hallucination claim (30% fewer responses with errors), the charts without printed values (SWE-Bench Pro, MRCR, CharXiv, ScreenSpot-Pro, tau2-bench) and pricing.

publications.name: Introducing GPT-5.1 for developers
publications.coverage: The nine-row Appendix table and its footnote. The SWE-bench Verified chart by reasoning effort prints no values beyond the 76.3% in the text, and the token-count chart is relative; both are left out, as are the partner quotes and pricing.

publications.name: Gemini 3.1 Pro model card
publications.coverage: The Evaluation results table ("Results as of February 2026"): eighteen benchmarks on twenty value rows (Humanity's Last Exam, Terminal-Bench 2.0, tau2-bench and MRCR v2 print two rows each), six model columns with the effort in the header, the Notes column kept as setup text. "Not supported" cells are no observation. Left out: the safety evaluation deltas and the Frontier Safety table, which are not benchmark results.

publications.name: Gemini 3.5 Flash model card
publications.coverage: The Evaluation results table ("Results as of May 2026"): thirteen benchmarks on fourteen value rows (MRCR v2 prints two rows), six model columns, the category and Notes columns kept as setup text. Left out: the safety evaluation deltas, which are not benchmark results.

publications.name: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite model card
publications.coverage: The Evaluation results table ("Results as of July 2026"): seven benchmarks on nine value rows (CharXiv Reasoning and GDM-MRCR v2 print two rows each), four model columns, the Notes column kept as setup text. Left out: the two price rows and the safety evaluation deltas, which are not benchmark results.

publications.name: Gemini 3.6 Flash model card
publications.coverage: The Evaluation results table ("Results as of July 2026"): eight benchmarks on ten value rows (CharXiv Reasoning and GDM-MRCR v2 print two rows each), six model columns, the Notes column kept as setup text. Left out: the two price rows with their temporary-discount note and the safety evaluation deltas, which are not benchmark results.

publications.name: Gemma 4 model card
publications.coverage: The "Benchmark Results" table of the model card: seventeen value rows under the headings Text, Vision, Audio and Long Context, six model columns (five Gemma 4 sizes and Gemma 3 27B marked "no think"). All models are the publisher's own; the footnote "*Excluding Chinese language" on the 12B audio cells is kept on those observations. Left out: the model data, safety and usage sections, which carry no benchmark values.

publications.name: Grok 4.1 Fast and Agent Tools API
publications.coverage: The text table under "The best agent for deep research": three benchmarks (Research-Eval by Reka, FRAMES, X Browse) with a Score and an Avg. Cost column each, four model rows. Scores are stored in the unit the page prints (a bare number) and costs in USD per task. Left out: the tau2-bench Telecom and Berkeley Function Calling v4 charts, whose values are drawn and not printed; the two "Multi Turn" charts, which print values but name no benchmark; the FActScore sentence, which prints no value; the price list.

publications.name: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 model card
publications.coverage: The single comparison table of the Introduction: ten benchmark rows (HLE prints "wo / w tools" in one cell, stored as two observations), eight model columns. The two DSBench rows are DeepSeek-internal test sets and are kept as such. Left out: the chat template and serving sections, which carry no values.

publications.name: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 model card
publications.coverage: The single comparison table of the Introduction: nine benchmark rows, five model columns. The two DSBench rows are DeepSeek-internal test sets. Left out: the chat template and serving sections, which carry no values.

publications.name: DeepSeek-V4-Pro (preview) model card
publications.coverage: Three tables of "Evaluation Results". Base Model: 24 benchmark rows with the metric in the label and a shot count per row, three DeepSeek base models. "DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max vs Frontier Models": 22 rows, six columns whose headers name the reasoning effort (Max, xHigh, High, Thinking). "Comparison across Modes": the same rows for V4-Flash and V4-Pro at Non-Think, High and Max; the V4-Pro Max column repeats the frontier table and is stored once, from that table. Left out: the architecture and parameter rows, the model download table, the reasoning-mode description table, the performance chart image, the chat template.

publications.name: DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp model card
publications.coverage: The comparison table of the Introduction: fourteen benchmark rows in two sections ("Reasoning Mode w/o Tool Use", "Agentic Tool Use"), two DeepSeek models. Left out: the running instructions, kernels and license sections, which carry no values.

Three results that the GPT-6 Astra page printed under a Claude Fable heading, with a footnote naming Claude Mythos, moved from their own identities to Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1. The footnote stays on each result.

Family descriptions checked against the maintainer or developer page for 29 families; every non-English string in the database and the research catalog rewritten in English; the Russian category fields removed.
Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 release page, performance table: Haiku 5.5, Haiku 4.5, GPT-6 Luna and Sonnet 5.5 (printed for reference) on eight rows.

Anthropic Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 release page, comparison table: Fable 5.1, Fable 5, Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on ten rows; the Mythos 5.1 value printed in the Fable 5.1 Terminal-Bench 4.0 cell stays under Fable 5.1 with its label on the row.
Google DeepMind Gemini 3.8 Flash model card, results table: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra on fourteen benchmark rows.
